Faint
fānt
v. and adj. (rendering Hebrew ya'aph/'alaph, Greek ekluō/ekkakeō)
From Old French feindre, to feign or shrink back, hence to give way, to lose heart. The Hebrew words describe both bodily exhaustion and the collapse of courage, and the Greek ekluō means literally to be loosed out — the strings of a man slackened until he can no longer hold together.

Biblical Definition

To faint in Scripture is to run out — of strength, of courage, or of endurance — and God's dealings with fainting men are among the tenderest passages in the Bible. Isaiah sets the promise against the plain fact of human limit: “He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength” (Isaiah 40:29), and then the great promise that follows: “they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). Note the descending order — mounting, running, walking — ending not with ecstasy but with the ordinary plod that outlasts everything. Paul applies the same word to the long obedience of well-doing: “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Galatians 6:9). And the Lord Jesus gives fainting as the alternative to praying: He “spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luke 18:1). That verse fixes the doctrine. There are only two responses to a burden that exceeds a man's strength: he prays, or he faints. Prayer is not a technique for the strong but the appointed refuge of those who have already discovered they cannot.

Webster 1828 Definition

To lose strength or courage; to sink into dejection or swoon; also weak, languid, dim. In Scripture, God giving power to the faint, those who wait on the LORD walking and not fainting, the command not to be weary in well doing, and the parable teaching men to pray and not to faint.

expand to see more

FAINT, a. 1. Weak; languid; inclined to swoon; destitute of strength.

2. Wanting courage or spirit; dejected; depressed; timorous.

3. Not bright or vivid; dim; as, a faint colour, a faint light.

4. From Old French feindre, to shrink or give way; the primary sense is to yield or fail.

5. In Scripture, they shall walk, and not faint, Isa. 40; men ought always to pray, and not to faint, Luke 18.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 40:29 — "He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength."

Isaiah 40:31 — "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

Galatians 6:9 — "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not."

Luke 18:1 — "And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;"

Modern Corruption

Weariness in the Christian life is reclassified as a wound to be treated rather than a weakness to be brought to God, so that the promised remedy of waiting on the LORD is replaced by rest technique, self-care, and the counsel to expect less of oneself.

expand to see more

Therapy-culture vocabulary has largely taken over the way churches speak about exhaustion. What Scripture calls fainting is now burnout, depletion, or an empty cup, and the prescriptions follow the diagnosis: boundaries, self-care, and a reduced expectation of duty. Some of that counsel is ordinary wisdom — the body has limits, Elijah under the juniper tree was fed and made to sleep before he was reasoned with, and God remembers that we are dust. But the biblical remedy is never merely the removal of demand. Isaiah's promise is renewal of strength in the running and the walking, given to those who wait upon the LORD, which is an activity of faith and not a suspension of it; and the Lord's answer to fainting is a parable about a widow who kept coming. Where the modern counsel stops at rest, Scripture sends the weary man to the throne of grace to find help in time of need.

The opposite error is to preach endurance as though it were self-generated, so that a fainting believer concludes he must try harder and is crushed by a standard no one can carry. Galatians 6:9 is not a demand for grit; it is a promise attached to a harvest — in due season we shall reap — and the season is God's to appoint. The principle to recover joins both halves: strength for the ordinary walk is real, is promised, and is God's gift, given not to the mighty but expressly to them that have no might. That is why perseverance is a doctrine of grace and not a virtue of the strong, and why the saints who last longest are usually those who learned earliest that they could not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ya'aph, to be weary or faint; 'alaph, to be overcome or swoon; Greek ekluō, to be loosed out or exhausted, and ekkakeō, to lose heart.

expand to see more

Hebrew ya'aph (H3286) — to be weary, to faint; used of the young men who shall utterly fall in Isaiah 40:30.

Hebrew 'alaph (H5968) — to cover, and thence to faint or swoon; Jonah fainted when the sun beat on his head (Jonah 4:8).

Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look for with expectation; the verb behind “they that wait upon the LORD” (Isaiah 40:31).

Greek ekluō (G1590) — to loose out, to relax utterly, to faint; used of the multitude who would faint by the way (Matthew 15:32).

Greek ekkakeō (G1573) — to lose heart, to grow weary in doing; the verb of Galatians 6:9 and Luke 18:1.

Usage

"Of strength given to the exhausted: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength (Isaiah 40:29)."

"Of perseverance in ordinary duty: in due season we shall reap, if we faint not (Galatians 6:9)."

"Of the alternative to prayer: men ought always to pray, and not to faint (Luke 18:1)."
